package_info.package_versions: N/A (open-source and paid variants, specific version not stated)
package_info.why_malicious: ExelaStealer is designed to steal sensitive information from Windows hosts, including credentials, system information, clipboard data, and screenshots, and exfiltrate this data to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Its code is intentionally obfuscated, and it masquerades as legitimate processes while performing unauthorized data collection and exfiltration.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes system commands to collect the Windows version and the host's hardware UUID, then stores this information for later exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting system version and hardware UUID is a common reconnaissance step for malware to fingerprint the victim machine.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely collects hardware UUIDs and system versions without user consent or clear purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise asset management tools may collect such data for inventory purposes.
key_indicators: Execution of system commands for host fingerprinting

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code attempts to extract image data from the clipboard and save it as a PNG file in a temporary directory named after the host's UUID.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and saving clipboard image data is a privacy risk and is rarely performed by legitimate applications without explicit user action.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not silently extract and store clipboard images in hidden directories.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Screenshot utilities may save clipboard images, but typically with user interaction.
key_indicators: Saving to hidden, UUID-named temp directory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c "echo ####System Info#### & systeminfo & echo ####System Version#### & ver & echo ####Host Name#### & hostname & echo ####Environment Variable#### & set & echo ####Logical Disk#### & wmic logicaldisk get caption,description,providername & echo ####User Info#### & net user & echo ####Startup Info#### & wmic startup get caption,command & echo ####Firewallinfo#### & netsh firewall show state "
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects extensive system information, including OS details, environment variables, disk info, user accounts, startup programs, and firewall status, and stores this data for exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Bulk collection of system and user information is a hallmark of infostealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not aggregate such a wide range of sensitive system data without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System diagnostic tools may collect some of this data, but typically with user awareness.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
netsh wlan export profile
C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c "netsh wlan show profile"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code exports and enumerates all saved WLAN profiles on the system, potentially exposing Wi-Fi credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exporting WLAN profiles can reveal Wi-Fi credentials, which is sensitive information.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not access or export WLAN profiles without explicit user intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Network troubleshooting tools may access WLAN profiles, but not silently.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Files are packaged into a Zip archive using the UUID as the filename, then sent using a Discord webhook (https://discord.com/api/webhooks/1139506512302194789/X_VYZdAHscWQ)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After data collection, the code compresses all gathered files into a zip archive and exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled Discord channel via a webhook.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating sensitive data to a third-party service (Discord) is a clear sign of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not send user/system data to Discord webhooks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Bug reporting tools may upload logs, but never to Discord webhooks.
key_indicators: Use of Discord webhook for exfiltration
Automated zipping and upload of sensitive data

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of the dropper binary, which unpacks and runs the main ExelaStealer payload and displays a decoy PDF.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the main infostealer logic

attack_chain.action: Collection of system version and hardware UUID for victim fingerprinting.
attack_chain.leads_to: Further system and user data collection

attack_chain.action: Extraction and saving of clipboard image data.
Bulk collection of system, user, disk, environment, and firewall information.
Export and enumeration of WLAN profiles to potentially steal Wi-Fi credentials.
Packaging of all collected data into a zip archive named after the host UUID.
Exfiltration of the zip archive to an attacker-controlled Discord webhook.
attack_chain.leads_to: Completion of attack; attacker receives stolen data

behavioral_signatures: Execution of system reconnaissance commands (systeminfo, wmic, net user, netsh)
Silent clipboard access and saving of clipboard images
Export of WLAN profiles without user interaction
Packaging of user/system data into zip archives in temp directories
Network communication to Discord webhooks for data exfiltration
file_indicators: Temporary directories in %TEMP% named after UUIDs
Zip archives in temp folders with UUID-based names
network_indicators: Outbound connections to Discord webhook endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for processes (especially those masquerading as legitimate Windows executables) that execute system reconnaissance commands, access clipboard data, export WLAN profiles, or create zip archives in temp directories. Flag any outbound network traffic to Discord webhook URLs, especially if accompanied by recent file compression activity. Look for the presence of known file indicators such as 'sirket-ruhsat-pdf.exe', 'Obfuscated.py', and UUID-named zip files in temp folders.
